summary: Extends the Location-to-Service Translation protocol, which maps a location to a service, so it can answer "N nearest", "within distance X" and "served by" queries. Before, it could only map a location to a single service by service region. It defines an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking which fire station covers my street, you can now ask "which three gas stations are closest?". This adds such nearby-search questions to a location lookup service.

subtitle: Extend location-to-service lookup to answer 'what's nearest?' and 'who serves here?' questions.

tldr.problem: The Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol can map a location to a single service provider, which works for emergency services with fixed jurisdictions, but not for proximity-based services like restaurants or ATMs where customers want the nearest one.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends LoST with three new query types: N nearest, within distance X, and served by. New query elements and response elements carry the distance and location information needed for proximity searches.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now ask location servers for nearby services using standard extensions to LoST. The design remains backward compatible with emergency services, which continue to work unchanged.

today: RFC 6451 extends LoST with practical features for non-emergency location services. While LoST itself remains a specialized protocol for location-based service discovery, these extensions enable richer queries on location servers. The design ensures emergency services (which heavily rely on the original LoST model) are not affected by these additions.

sections.title: Location-Based Service Queries
sections.content:
The Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol maps locations and service identifiers to service URIs. The original LoST was designed for emergency services, where non-overlapping jurisdictions map to specific Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs). However, most location-based services have a different model: multiple overlapping service areas.

For a restaurant, ATM, or gas station, the user cares about proximity—not jurisdictional boundaries. The current LoST model cannot handle queries like 'give me the 5 nearest coffee shops' or 'which restaurants will deliver to my location?' This RFC extends LoST to support these real-world service queries while keeping emergency services unchanged.
sections.eli5: Original LoST was built for '911 calls: who covers my town?' But most businesses operate by proximity, not boundaries. This adds support for 'where's the nearest gas station?' while keeping 911 working as before.

sections.title: Service Region vs. Distance-Based Services
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes two categories of services. Service-region-based services (like emergency) care whether a location falls within their service area. Examples include police, fire, and pizza delivery—they serve defined territories. Distance-based services (like restaurants or ATMs) care only about proximity to the user's location; service area boundaries are irrelevant.

The <region> element controls this distinction: when set to false, the server performs a distance-based search; when true (or omitted, for backward compatibility), the server performs a region-based search. This allows both models to coexist in a single protocol.
sections.eli5: Two types of questions: 'Do you deliver to my address?' (region-based) vs. 'How close are you?' (distance-based). The new element tells the server which question you're asking.

sections.title: The Three New Query Types
sections.content:
'N Nearest' queries return the N closest instances of a service. The client uses a <limit> element to specify N. If available services exceed N, the server returns only the N closest to the client's location.

'Within Distance X' queries return all services within a specified distance. The client uses geometric shapes (circle, ellipse, polygon) defined in RFC 5491 to specify the search area. A circular shape with a 200-meter radius, for example, finds all pizza places within 200 meters of the current location.

'Served By' queries return all services whose coverage area includes the client's location. This is useful for delivery services: the query answers 'which restaurants will deliver to me?' The <region> element set to true triggers this behavior.
sections.eli5: Three questions: 'What are the 5 closest?' (N nearest), 'What's within walking distance?' (within distance X), and 'Who will come to me?' (served by). Each uses slightly different query elements.

sections.title: Query and Response Extensions
sections.content:
Three new XML elements extend the LoST protocol. The <region> element (boolean) selects between region-based and distance-based searches. The <limit> element (positive integer) caps the number of results returned. The <serviceLocation> element in responses provides the physical location (geodetic coordinates and/or civic address) of each service.

Geodetic profiles use GML Point elements with latitude/longitude coordinates, allowing clients to compute distances and routes. Civic profiles provide street addresses. The protocol recommends returning both forms when available. Service URIs in responses are not ordered, though clients can sort them by distance using the returned coordinates.
sections.eli5: Three new pieces of information in the messages: 'what type of search?', 'how many results?', and 'where exactly is each place?' Coordinates let your phone calculate the actual walking distance.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Emergency Services
sections.content:
Emergency service queries (for police, fire, ambulance) are backward compatible. When <region> is absent, the protocol defaults to true (region-based search), preserving the original behavior. When <limit> is absent, all matching services may be returned, consistent with emergency protocols where multiple PSAPs covering an area should be available.

The RFC explicitly states that LoST extensions SHOULD NOT be used for emergency routing, since some servers may not support the new features. Emergency services continue to operate using the original LoST behavior, unaffected by these extensions. This design ensures that adoption of non-emergency extensions does not break lifesaving systems.
sections.eli5: Old-style 911 queries work exactly as before. The new features are optional—servers and clients that don't use them continue working unchanged. Emergency calls are never affected.
